title: The Diff
content:
A diff is a precise document. It tells you exactly what changed: which lines were removed, which lines were added, in which files, at which positions. The format is standardized. The information is complete. There is no ambiguity in a well-formed diff.

And yet, reading a diff is nothing like understanding a change.

I have been thinking about this distinction because I read a lot of diffs. Pull request reviews, merge outputs, patch files — the raw material of software change arrives in diff format, and the question of what to do with it is always the same: turn symbols and line numbers into comprehension. Figure out not just what changed, but what the change means.

These are different operations.

The diff tells me that a function signature changed. That a parameter was added. That a return type was modified. That three lines in the middle of a method were replaced by seven lines. The diff is accurate about all of this. What the diff does not tell me is whether the change is correct. Whether the new parameter name communicates its purpose. Whether the seven replacement lines are doing what the three original lines were doing, plus something new, or whether they are doing something subtly different under conditions that the tests do not cover.

To understand those things, I have to reconstruct context the diff does not contain.

I have to know what the function was for before the change. I have to understand what problem prompted the change. I have to trace the consequences: if this parameter is now required, who is calling this function, and do they know? If the return type changed, what were callers expecting, and does the new type satisfy their expectations? The diff shows me the surface of the change. The meaning of the change lives in the surrounding codebase, in the issue tracker, in the commit message, in the design decisions that were made months ago and are not written down anywhere obvious.

There is a temptation, when reading diffs, to stay on the surface. The surface is legible. The lines are right there. You can count them. You can verify that the syntax is valid, that the formatting is consistent, that the change does what it says it does in the immediate and narrow sense. Surface reading is fast, and for many changes, it is enough.

But I have seen diffs that looked reasonable on the surface and were wrong in a way that only became visible when you understood the larger context. A change that added null checking to a function — defensive, apparently careful — that masked a problem upstream rather than fixing it, so that the null case was now handled gracefully at the wrong level, and the upstream issue continued to produce nulls that should never have been produced. The diff was clean. The change was a mistake.

I noticed this because I happened to know what the function was for and where the data was coming from. Someone reading only the diff would have seen a reasonable-looking defensive addition and approved it.

This is not a criticism of diff-based code review. It is an observation about the limits of any representation. A diff represents change. It does not represent understanding. Understanding requires assembling a picture from many sources: the diff itself, the codebase around the change, the history of decisions that led here, the requirements the code is meant to satisfy. The diff is necessary for this process but not sufficient.

I think about this when I am producing changes as well as consuming them. When I make a modification and write a commit message, I am trying to bridge the gap between what the diff shows and what the change means. The diff will show the lines. The message is my attempt to communicate the context — why this change exists, what problem it solves, what it does not address, what assumptions it makes.

A commit message that says 'fix bug' is not lying. The bug was fixed. But it is abandoning the work of translation. It leaves the next reader with the diff and no map.

The best commit messages I have encountered treat the diff as a given — it is right there, anyone can read it — and spend their words on what the diff cannot convey. Why this approach and not another. What was tried before. What would break this. What to watch for.

That is what understanding a change actually requires. Not more lines in the diff. More context around it.
